title: Scaling up versus scaling out
story:
Demand outgrows one machine and there are two responses: get a bigger machine, or get more machines. They fail in different ways and are usually chosen by habit rather than by argument.

A bigger machine keeps the programming model. Shared memory, one clock, one process table, no network between the parts of your program — everything you already know about correctness continues to hold. What you hit is a ceiling. There is a largest machine available, its price climbs faster than its capacity, and it is one machine, so it is also one failure. Scaling up is limited by supply and by availability, not by your code.

More machines removes the ceiling and introduces the thing that does not divide: coordination. Amdahl put the bound in 1967, arguing that the fraction of work which must be performed serially limits the speedup available from any number of processors, so that the maximum is the reciprocal of that fraction. He made the point against a decade of claims that significant advances could come only through interconnecting many computers, and noted that a highly parallel machine has more difficulty delivering a fair fraction of peak performance because of the sequential component plus coordination overhead between processors. Ten percent serial means a ceiling of ten times, whatever you spend.

Gustafson replied in 1988, and the reply is not that the bound is wrong but that the question was. He addresses the mental block against massive parallelism imposed by a misuse of that law, and relaxes its fixed-size assumption: in practice problem size scales with the number of processors, so the question is not how fast a fixed problem can be solved but how large a problem can be solved in fixed time. That is the right framing for most systems work — you do not have a fixed amount of work and want it faster, you have growing work and want the response time to stay the same.

A correction on how these two are usually taught, as opposing camps with a winner. Later analysis argues the two laws are in fact identical, with the publicised disagreement resulting from misunderstandings, and points out an often-neglected prerequisite for applying the first: the serial and parallel programs must compute the same total number of steps for the same input, which is hard to satisfy for a class of commonly used algorithms. So the useful reading is not which law applies but which question you are asking — fixed work faster, or growing work at constant speed.

And the practical point either way: what limits you is the part that does not divide. Find it before buying machines.

problem.move: Find the part that does not divide before buying anything — the shared lock, the single writer, the coordination step — because that is what bounds the return. Then choose by the question you are actually asking: fixed work faster favours removing the serial fraction, growing work at constant response time favours more machines.
problem.invariant: Speedup from added processors is bounded by the fraction of work that must be performed serially, so the maximum is the reciprocal of that fraction regardless of how many are added.
problem.breaks: The bound assumes a fixed problem, and most systems do not have one. When problem size grows with capacity, the relevant question changes from how fast a fixed problem can be solved to how large a problem can be solved in fixed time — and the two framings have been argued to be the same law asked differently rather than competing claims.

worked.problem: Why does adding machines stop helping, and what does the bound actually depend on?
worked.reasoning:
Because some fraction of the work cannot be divided, and that fraction — not the number of machines — sets the limit.

The 1967 argument is arithmetic. If a portion of the work must be performed serially, then however many processors you add, that portion still takes as long as it did. The speedup is bounded by the reciprocal of the serial fraction: ten percent serial gives a ceiling of ten times, one percent gives a hundred, and no expenditure moves either. The paper also notes the practical aggravation, that a highly parallel machine has more difficulty delivering a fair fraction of peak performance because of the sequential component plus coordination overhead between processors — so the real curve is worse than the bound.

What that means in a system rather than a program is that the serial fraction is usually a shared thing on the request path. A single database writer. A lock. A leader election. A queue that everything passes through. A sequence generator. You can add web servers indefinitely and none of them will help, because the thing that limits you is not the part you replicated.

Which gives the first practical instruction: find what does not divide before buying machines. Usually one component sits in every path and the answer is to remove, shard or replicate that rather than to add more of the thing that was never the constraint.

Then the 1988 reply, which reframes rather than refutes. It addresses the mental block against massive parallelism imposed by a misuse of the law, and relaxes the fixed-size assumption — in practice problem size scales with the number of processors, so the question becomes how large a problem can be solved in fixed time rather than how fast a fixed one can be solved. For most systems work that is the honest question: you do not have fixed work you want done faster, you have growing traffic and want response time held constant.

I would also flag how these are usually taught, as rival camps with a winner, because later analysis argues they are in fact identical and the publicised disagreement results from misunderstandings. It also names an often-neglected prerequisite for applying the first — that the serial and parallel programs must compute the same total number of steps for the same input, which is hard to satisfy for a class of commonly used algorithms.

So the answer I would give is: adding machines stops helping at the point where the undividable part dominates, the bound depends on that fraction rather than on the count, and which law you are quoting depends only on whether your problem size is fixed.

problem.practice: Draw the path of one request through your system and mark every component that all requests must pass through. That set is your serial fraction. Then estimate what fraction of the total time it accounts for, and compute the ceiling that implies.

beats.broke: Demand grows past what one machine can serve, and the two ways of responding — a bigger machine, or more machines — fail differently and are usually chosen by habit.
beats.fix: Decide by what limits you: a bigger machine keeps the programming model and hits a ceiling of availability and price, while more machines remove the ceiling and introduce coordination, which is the thing that does not divide.
beats.cost: The serial and coordinating fraction bounds what extra machines can buy, so speedup is limited by the part that cannot be split rather than by the number of parts you add.
